text: A family pools everything it owns and hands the bundle to its most hopeful son, who sets out for Istanbul and arrives with nothing. Kazan gives that reversal 174 minutes, and the length is the argument: the distance between an Anatolian village and a berth on a westbound ship is not a montage but an accumulation of small defeats, each one paid for in money the boy no longer has. The Academy's award went to the art direction, a decorative-sounding credit for a picture in which rooms and streets have to carry a household's standing, a wage, the difference between a guest and a servant. Black and white, 1963, an American director going back to Anatolia for a story about wanting out of it. America itself stays a rumor for a very long time.

A sports agent has second thoughts about the work, says so out loud, and within days has one client left. What follows isn't redemption in the usual shape; it is 139 minutes of a man finding out how much of his charm was a function of his phone list. Cameron Crowe writes people who talk their way toward what they feel and then get caught by it, and the running joke here is a professional persuader who can no longer persuade, least of all Rod Tidwell, the football player who stayed and who wants more than an agent can hand over. The Writers Guild put the screenplay on its list of 101, which is the right credit: what lasts is phrasing and timing, the beat before somebody answers. It is famous enough that the lines arrive pre-worn. The film underneath them is smaller, and far more anxious about money.

Secrets keep badly in the heat, and the summer of 1962 runs long in this corner of Louisiana. Kasi Lemmons puts a family's private arrangements - what was done, who saw it, what was agreed to in silence - inside a house where a child is always in the next room, and then lets the child do the looking. It moves at the pace of a season rather than a plot: 108 minutes in which the Batistes go about their business and the business becomes unbearable to one person at a time. Lemmons is patient with ordinary hours, which is why the betrayals land as betrayals rather than incidents, and she trusts a household to have its own laws of memory and blame without explaining them to anybody. The National Film Registry has it. Whatever this family has kept from itself, the film is in no hurry to hand over.

Eighteen years on a mountain farm, and then a funeral makes the lowlands compulsory. What Jim Craig owes is specific: the family place has to be earned back before it can be lived on, and the wages are all downhill. George T. Miller directs a Western with no frontier left to push at - the country below is claimed, fenced and staffed - so the drama runs on employment, other men's horses, and how a boy from up there gets read by people down here. The Australian academy gave it the cinematography award, which in a picture built on riding is less a decoration than a verdict on the riding. Romance and adventure are both in it, unembarrassed, at a tempo that assumes an audience will sit still for weather. A hundred and four minutes, and the mountain is patient.

The river has no opinion about the three girls growing up on its bank, and the film takes that indifference seriously. Renoir shot on location in India, in color for the first time in his career, and the color is less applied to the picture than found in the place. Adapted from a novel by Rumer Godden, it follows three young women through the year in which feeling arrives - jealousy, vanity, the first serious wanting - while the Bengal water outside goes on doing what it did the year before, at the same speed. Two clocks run at once. The slower one never hurries, and the film refuses to rank a girl's worst afternoon below it, or above it. Ninety-nine minutes, made in 1951 by a French production that had to travel a very long way to get its light.

Fifty minutes, 1916, and the whole weight of it rests on the price of one pair of shoes. Lois Weber built a film in which a wage is the plot: a shopgirl's salary feeds a household, the household spends it, and the leather on her feet thins a little more with every walk to work. There is no villain in that arithmetic, which is the hard part - only the distance between what a week pays and what a body needs, closing at the rate of a few cents. Weber directs the wanting plainly, as wanting and not as symbol, and lets the shoes stay shoes. The National Film Registry keeps it. Silent, short, more than a century old, and still exact about the thing films of any era go vague on: how much money, by when, and what a person does in the meantime.

The heist goes fine; the money turns out to be counterfeit. That disappointment is the engine - Lupin the Third and his partner Jigen go looking for whoever prints bills that good, and the trail ends at a castle with a prisoner inside it. Miyazaki keeps the caper's manners intact: the thief flirts, the law pursues, the plan is withheld until it has already worked. His invention goes into architecture, treating the castle as a machine with a route through it rather than a backdrop with a door, and the pleasure is physical - weight, momentum, a chase permitted to pause so that one movement can be watched properly. Kinema Junpo's all-time list of Japanese films is a formal room for a picture about a burglar, and this one sits in it without straightening its tie.

A man cuts himself open to push metal into the wound, and the wound answers with maggots. He runs into the road, a commuter hits him, and the driver and his girlfriend hide the body. From there the film is closer to a process than a plot: infection at industrial speed, a body retooled with parts nobody ordered. Tsukamoto pitches the first minute high and then refuses to come down, and the noise is not accompaniment, it is most of the argument. Horror and science fiction both fit the thing and both sound too calm beside it. What frightens is not an event but a rate - flesh has a schedule now, and nobody can slow it. Sixty-seven minutes is about as much of that as a person can take, and the film appears to know it exactly.

The killers in this are ranked, and the hero is number three. A job goes wrong and the ranking turns into a hunting order, the man above him being a position rather than a person, so the whole trade reveals itself as a league table with bullets. Suzuki's 91 minutes keep the assignment and throw out the manners: continuity gives way to composition, the murders are staged as design problems with a correct solution, and private appetites take up the screen time another crime picture would spend on motive. It is funny the way total conviction is funny. Holding it together is a professional's predicament - a man whose competence is the only self he has, watching it get outranked from above - and the film is most alert when he is least.

The offer is a post running labour at a mine in Manchuria, and what comes attached to it is exemption from military service. Kaji takes it, and takes his new wife Michiko with him. That bargain is the whole argument: a man who has just written honestly about the treatment of Chinese workers is handed a chance to prove his ideas function, on condition that he becomes the person who administers them. Kobayashi needs 204 minutes because decency at that desk is not a position but a daily negotiation - with foremen who have their own methods, with officials who profit from the arrangement as it stands, with the military police behind both. Nothing here is metaphorical. It is a quota, a wage, a company town, a marriage conducted inside it. This is only the first part, and the arithmetic already runs against him.

Amateur baseball, a gas pump, and then a misunderstanding with the local yakuza that cannot be walked back. Masaki decides he needs a gun, which means Okinawa, which means a trip the film is in no rush to complete. Kitano puts the comedy in dead time - the standing around, the abrupt idiocy, the shot held past the point where a joke would ordinarily land - and lets the violence arrive without the courtesy of a build. In Okinawa the errand acquires Uehara, a gangster in debt to the men he intends to take revenge on, and much worse company than anything the boy has met at home. Ninety-six minutes. What it does to the crime picture is not parody but subtraction: the arranging goes, the swagger goes, the sense of occasion goes, and what is left is what a beating actually looks like.

Two boys at the back of the class, bored, casually cruel, better at each other's company than at anything school can offer them. They drop out. The paths split - one takes up boxing, one attaches himself to a gang - and each finds that his new world also has a back of the class, with seniors in it who decide how far a person gets. Kitano is unsentimental about talent: the subject here is the moment a young man is told his ceiling, by a trainer or by somebody further up the organization, and what he does in the months after being told. Friendship is neither betrayed nor kept; it is outrun by two schedules. A hundred and seven minutes, and the drift is the plot. These two were funny together, and the film goes on remembering it after they have stopped.

One room, more people in it than it can hold, and a ledger of debts nobody expects to see settled. Kurosawa keeps almost the whole of 125 minutes inside a rundown boardinghouse in nineteenth-century Japan: the thief Sutekichi, the landlady Osugi, her younger sister Okayo, an actor whose best work is behind him, an old man whose manner nobody can place. Talk is the event. In a house where everyone already knows exactly what everyone is, what a person claims to be becomes the only currency still circulating, and the film is comic about that for a long while. There is nothing to look at but faces and the short distances between them. A love triangle in such a place is less a plot than a match struck in a room with no ventilation.

Noriko Shimabara leaves her family in Toyokawa for a website, and the people on the website seem to have been expecting her. Kumiko runs the board, Haikyo.com, and also runs a circle that behaves the way a family behaves, with roles, duties and a place laid for the newcomer. Sono takes 159 minutes over this, and the length is not indulgence: it is how long a household needs in order to be replaced by another one without anyone raising a voice. The film is filed under horror and the label holds, though nothing chases anybody. What unsettles is the ease of the exchange - how little it costs a teenager to become the daughter of strangers, how fast the vocabulary of home is issued to someone who arrived on Tuesday. Japan, 2005, and a girl reading her own name as though it were a part.
